lesson.title: What Architecture Means
lesson.summary: Introduces architecture as the underlying structure of a system ,  its components, their relationships, and the reasoning behind key design choices ,  and explains why architectural decisions are unusually costly to reverse.
lesson.body:
Before you can evaluate any technology honestly, you need a word for the thing you're evaluating, and in this book that word is "architecture." Architecture isn't the code itself, and it isn't a feature list ,  it's the underlying shape of a system: what parts it's built from, how those parts communicate with each other, and the rules that govern how the whole thing is allowed to change over time. Think of it as the answer to the question, "if I opened this system up, what would I find inside, and why is it built this way rather than some other way?"

Consider a familiar example: a company deciding how to store its customer data. One architecture might put everything in a single database that every application reads from and writes to directly. Another might split the data across several smaller databases, each owned by a different team, with services passing messages between them instead of touching each other's data directly. Both approaches can serve the exact same customers and features on day one. What differs is how they behave as the company grows, hires more engineers, or needs to change one part of the system without breaking another. The single shared database is simple to reason about early on, but as more teams write to it, coordination gets harder, and a schema change one team makes can silently break another team's code. The split design costs more to build up front ,  it needs message-passing infrastructure and clearer ownership boundaries ,  but it tends to hold up better as complexity grows.

This is why architectural decisions are treated as higher-stakes than ordinary coding choices. A bug in a single function is usually cheap to fix: you find it, change a few lines, redeploy, and move on. An architectural decision, by contrast, gets embedded into dozens or hundreds of other decisions built on top of it. If a company chooses the single shared database and, years later, wants to switch to the split model, that isn't a quick refactor ,  it means rewriting how every team's code talks to data, migrating existing records, and running both systems in parallel while cutting over carefully so nothing breaks. The cost of undoing an architectural choice tends to grow with how much has already been built on top of it, not with how flawed the original choice turns out to be.

That asymmetry ,  cheap to choose, expensive to undo ,  is the entire reason this book spends time on architecture before evaluating any specific technology. Whether the system in question is a single company's backend, a nationwide payment network, or, as you'll encounter soon, a blockchain, the same pattern holds: someone made structural choices early about what components exist, how they connect, and what tradeoffs they were willing to accept, and those early choices now shape what the system can and cannot do cheaply later. Understanding architecture means being able to ask, of any system handed to you, three questions: what are the pieces, how do they relate to one another, and what did the designers give up in order to get the properties they wanted? Every method you'll learn later in this book for judging whether an architecture was a good one starts from being able to answer those three questions clearly.
